question: How precisely can we estimate the treatment effect at the true eligibility cutoff when the score has Gaussian measurement error but treatment is recorded reliably? Comparing outcomes near the observed cutoff mixes different true scores. Existing identification and asymptotic inference do not supply the requested coverage guarantee across an entire population class at every sample size.
result: The target is θ(P)=μ₁(P,0)−μ₀(P,0). Assume independent observations; known support [−1,1], noise scale σ∈[0,1], and smoothness exponent β∈(0,1]; independent standard Gaussian measurement error; continuous score density between 1/4 and 3/4; binary potential outcomes with continuous means between 1/4 and 3/4 satisfying |μ_d(x)−μ_d(t)|≤2|x−t|^β globally. Set ν=2β+1 and h₀=n^(−1/ν). Define Ψ(h,σ) as 0 when σ≤h, (σ/h)^(2/3)−1 when σ⁴≤h<σ, and h^(−1/2){1+log(σ²/√h)}−1 when h<σ⁴. The unique solution h★∈[h₀,1] to log n+ν log h★=Ψ(h★,σ) determines rβ=h★^β. Uniformly over n≥2 and σ∈[0,1], minimax expected absolute error Rβ and minimax worst-case expected length ℒβ of connected, uniformly 90%-covering intervals satisfy c rβ≤Rβ≤Eβ≤C rβ and c rβ≤ℒβ≤2Eβ≤C rβ. The construction attains these upper bounds, and c,C depend only on β.
mechanism: Treatment reveals which side of the true cutoff each observation occupies. Reflect the untreated side so both arms have endpoint zero on [0,1]. Construct nonnegative, normalized Chebyshev polynomial weights K_L concentrating near zero at distance of order L^(−2). Their smoothness moment M_{L,β} is at most C L^(−2β). For each arm, divide the weighted outcome integral A_{d,L} by the weighted density integral B_{d,L}. This gives a positive average near the cutoff; the density lower bound keeps its denominator away from zero, and smoothness bounds its bias. Replace K_L by the finite Gaussian correction Q_{L,σ}, whose conditional expectation at the noisy score equals K_L at the true score. Recorded treatment and observed outcomes then give unbiased empirical numerators and denominators. Floor empirical denominators and project arm estimates onto the maintained mean range, then subtract them. Gaussian second moments give V_L, a bound on sampling variability. Combine endpoint bias and sampling allowances in ρ_L=12M_{L,β}+28√(40V_L/n), and form an interval around the estimated effect. Choose L to minimize this public radius over a finite candidate set, including a trivial interval covering the whole admissible target range. For optimality, construct two smooth populations with different cutoff effects but perturbations whose low-order moments cancel, making their noisy observed distributions difficult to distinguish.
why_true: The treatment record preserves the true side even when the proxy cannot reliably locate the cutoff. Polynomial inversion exactly removes Gaussian blurring from the desired weights. Positive latent weights, bounded density, and global smoothness control bias; the Gaussian second-moment identity controls the price of inversion. Increasing polynomial order improves localization but increases sampling cost, yielding the resolution balance. Chebyshev’s inequality and a union bound provide finite-sample coverage, and selection using only known inputs preserves it. Conversely, moment-canceling perturbations change the endpoint mean while Gaussian smoothing conceals their observable differences. Nearby sample distributions prevent reliable estimation of their separation and force honest intervals to include both targets with substantial probability. The direct alternatives supply the remaining lower bound when noise is small or absent.
example: For β=1 and σ=n^(−1/6), the example stays in the intermediate regime for every n≥2. Both optimal estimation error and honest interval length have order n^(−1/6)/[1+(1/2)log n]^(3/2), compared with n^(−1/3) under direct score observation. This demonstrates that improving measurement can still leave a substantial precision penalty.

findings.problem: The two long inequality chains, informal statement, symbol explanations, and construction paragraph repeat the same conclusion and make the main theorem difficult to absorb on screen.
findings.fix: Display the shorter chains c rβ≤Rβ≤Eβ≤C rβ and c rβ≤ℒβ≤2Eβ≤C rβ. Add one sentence saying the constructed estimator and honest interval attain Eβ and 2Eβ, and retain the conditions and constant dependence.

findings.problem: “Why both bounds match” combines support selection, support saturation, a detailed χ² bound, sample indistinguishability, the interval argument, randomization, and the zero-noise case. The central lower-bound explanation competes with too many details.
findings.fix: Split the slide: first show how support selection and moment cancellation hide a cutoff separation of order h★^β; then show how the event-probability bound forces both estimation error and interval length. Put the zero-noise argument on the second slide and shorten the displayed bound by suppressing numerical constants.
